data.content_ref: inline:SRC_03's causal mechanism rests on an unsupported premise: that expert intuition generalizes to out-of-distribution cases while the checklist does not. But the problem concerns tasks with objectively verifiable outcomes, for which a checklist can encode decision rules causally sufficient for correctness (e.g., a diagnostic criterion or a scoring rubric). On such tasks, the expert's 'high-dimensional, non-verbalizable feature space' is not demonstrably causally relevant to the outcome; the checklist's verifiable rules are. SRC_003 provides no causal mechanism connecting tacit System 1 recognition to superior verifiable-outcome accuracy on OOD cases; it simply stipulates that the expert generalizes and the checklist does not. A checklist that encodes the causally operative features will generalize to OOD cases exactly when those features are present, and will fail exactly when the expert's intuition also lacks the relevant information. SRC_003's argument therefore does not establish the expert's superiority 'on average' for the task class the problem specifies.
